en: A people no man would wish to see.
Beijing is no easy place;
Your father Manas would not listen,
And led the armies of the world,
Leaving the village of sixty sons
And widowed women desolate!
Your wretched mother speaks—know this;
Oh, my only son, heed my words!
In teeming China,
There are the peoples of forty tribes;
Whoever attacks it, that Beijing
By custom drinks their blood.
Beijing is no easy place;
The Chinese are no people to toy with!
Mighty China is a powerful nation;
My dear son, know this:
When you see their multitude, they are black beetles!
If you wage holy war against the unbelievers,
My darling foal,
Hero Khan Kongurbai
Has a fortress beside the road;
The Kalcha whose road is barred
Has a lion who will answer you.
Do not dig my grave,
Forever refusing to listen;
Do not make my sorrows boil.
Forever refusing to heed
Your fathers and forefathers,
Do not show me such a spectacle!
My tiger son, hear my words!
Take able Bakai, who knows the road;
Take the stout-lunged, roaring,
The mighty who do not retreat from death,
Who spare themselves nothing.
Gather seven sacred banners,
Gather an army that makes the earth sag,
Then go to Beijing!
Take an army from the Muslims,
Take no small force, but many,
Then go to Beijing.
Fools merely say “Beijing”;
Those who know call it “Great Beijing”—
Beijing is no small place but vast.
On its front side is Bakburchun,
The mightiest of all is Kakan-Chin.
Most numerous is Shang-Kai, the great Manchu;
Consider how many cities there are.
If you ponder, that Beijing
Also has the aspect of a holy place.
Against great, afflicted Beijing,
Only then begin your conflict!
I do not approve of this departure;
Guard your own life yourself!
My soul mate, heed me,
Take the whole Muslim army!
Raising the Muslim battle cry,
Send the army against this China!
Gathering a great dark host,
If you set out for Kakan-Chin,
Who will be left with this regret?
Turn back, enter, and wage enmity,
Then bring great conflict upon Kakan!
Saying, “I shall gird my waist firmly,”
You have grown impassioned,
Saying, “From the Kalcha in Beijing,
I shall exact my father's blood-price.”
Such is the nature of the journey;
Understand my words without making me lament!
May your journey be in the cool autumn;
May your enemy Kongurbai, whom you will spear,
Stand on a plain as small as a palm.
Of the giant you have longed for,
If I tell his qualities, let them be countless;
When you enter battle lamenting,
May the spirit of your lion father,
Your bloodthirsty hero, stand beside you!
Your father's sworn friend Almambet,
Akbaltai's Chubak,
Syrgak, born a lion—
In the midst of that battle,
May those soul-companions be your aid!
When you advance and extend your spear,
May all the heroes be present!
I am your mother Kanykei;
Receive the counsel of this unfortunate woman,
Take the Muslim army!
Against the seething unbelievers,
Against hero Khan Kongurbai,
Advance thus and begin the conflict!
If you gather them, you have many troops;
Against the seething unbelievers,
You have fine men who can clash.
Let me tell of the hero
Who dwells yonder in Sary-Arka;
No man has defeated him in combat either.
If you ask his father and lineage:
His lattice walls and roof poles are of wood,
His first ancestor was Alach;
Hero Kökchö, son of Aidarkan—
The heel of the blue boot,
Kökchö of the Kazakhs.
Broth rich with meat, fatty flesh,
His warriors are set apart,
Broad-chested and red-faced,
He overwhelmed every enemy he met,
And winnowed their millet clean,
Those who praise their wives like maidens—
Such are the boastful Kazakh people,
Such are the men to bind at your waist.
At the word “enemy” they bolt forward,
Brandishing tufted spears;
When they descend into a river valley, they cry aloud,
Singing their ölöng and raising a din.
A formidable people of grave custom,
They do not stand idle at the word “enemy.”
Ümötöi, son of Kökchö,
Is of the same year as you,
Equal to you in age;
Ümötöi and you
Are cousins through your mothers.
Ümötöi, son of Kökchö—
Unless he proves a true dog,
If you ride to Beijing, his road is with yours.
He is kin to you;
His poor mother Akerkech
Shared a nest with Kanykei,
Of the same root and lineage,
And so he is your kinsman.
Unless he proves the worst of dogs,
He will pursue the blood-price of his father Kökchö!
I have more words, more still;
Let me tell of the people as a whole:
Beyond Bukhara and Sharip,
On this side of ruined Chambyl,
With a warrior’s gear filling an embrace,
Is Muzburchak, son of Buudaiyk Khan,
From the fascinating land beyond the pass,
From the people called Kyiva.
Buyanbek, son of Muzburchak,
Was left with little sense,
Left young when his father died.
Burulkan, whom Muzburchak married,
Shared a nest with me.
Buyanbek, son of Muzburchak,
Would properly be
Your cousin through your mothers.
Those peoples of Kyiva
No one has conquered,
No enemy has brought under submission.
Such is the nature of their land;
Their caps are an armful across.
At every hero’s side
Hangs a great knife broad as a breast.
Heed the words of your mother Kanykei
And take Buyanbek himself.
He is the renowned one, that is the man,
The hero to bind at your waist.
Against the infidels of the Kakanchin,
Against hero Khan Kongurbai,
He is the man who will go on campaign.
My son, Beijing is no easy land;
You have begun a campaign to Beijing,
Leaving your mother crying aloud,
Leaving the poor woman here behind!
Beijing with Kaspang is a black city,
And has many places of battle.
They say Beijing is a strong land,
No mortal who faced it has prevailed.
Great Beijing, where the sun rises,
Has heat that gives no respite.
There is no good in this undertaking;
You have no coat to wear against the heat!
As I have learned from tradition,
Mortals cannot endure the heat;
They say a person’s eyes glaze over,
And a cauldron set upon the sand
Boils rumbling without fire.
In the blink of an eye,
Before one can say this or that,
Of the water in the cauldron,
Not a spoonful remains, they say.
Swift foot soldiers without clothing—
Kongurbai’s numerous army
Throngs that desert, they say;
Of anyone who goes there to fight,
Not a spoonful of blood remains, they say.
Of Kakanchin’s Beijing,
From the reports we have heard and learned,
On this side lie Dyngsha and the gray night;
For anyone who challenges
The Kakanchin Chinese, it becomes black night.
You would not heed
Your poor mother, my hero and only one;
You stopped me at the gate,
Cast your mother into desolation,
And made me lament the Kakanchin.
You would have me sing my lament;
Never heeding my words,
You would make your poor mother
Speak the truth within me!
The robed sheikhs and blue-robed attendants,
The chosen men of Kokon and Margalang,
With wound turbans upon their heads,
Pleading to the Almighty—
Let me tell of their way of life:
They have round-baked bread,
And houses built with four corners.
If you gather them as your support,
There are also the people of four khans.
If you muster them for Beijing, they are humble folk,
All a pack-camel-riding frontier people.
If you go to Beijing, gather an army;
Gather many as your support!
In renowned Beijing
There are the Black Kalmak people;
Among those people,
If you fight them, my champion,
There are giants of many kinds.
Among those giants
Are skilled men who level spears,
And masters able to cast the noose without missing
In the darkness of the moon,
Men perfected in their craft.
Against seething Beijing,
When you charge and level your spear,
Saying, “I shall avenge my khan father,”
And turn your whole body without restraint,
While guns fire and bows are drawn,
And weapons clash together,
Will the Chinese not truly reach you?
If you take no support beside you,
Will your life not be left without recourse?
They have jang-juns and Torguts;
They have Shibe and Solon.
The forty speak forty different tongues,
The forty tribes of distinguished Chinese.
I have said many words; heed my speech,
My only one blessed by Kydyr, understand!
When his mother spoke in this way,
The gray wolf surged and could not stand still,
Coiling like a dragon,
His eyes burning like embers.
The young champion, son of the bloodletter,
Had Kongurbai as the foe he would fight;
It was time for him to go to Kakan.
With broad teeth like a gate,
Such teeth as no people possessed,
Teeth unlike those of any other tribe,
He bared them white,
And, refusing to heed his mother,
Answered her with harsh words:
“Mother, who would listen to these words of yours?
Let some black night listen!
Tormenting the people to gather an army,
Making some of them weep,
Forcing some by violence,
